📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The United States has officially lost its measles elimination status, a major public health achievement that was secured 26 years ago.

Recent findings suggest that the Pan American Health Organization (PAHO), the World Health Organization’s (WHO) regional office for the Americas, determined that measles has spread continuously in the U.S. for more than 12 months. On November 17, PAHO revealed the end of the country’s measles elimination status, which it has held since 2000.

It has been revealed that “Losing a measles elimination status has broader implications than losing a public health designation,” PAHO’s director, Jarbas Barbosa, MD, MPH, PhD, remarked in a media briefing. “It means the virus has circulated for a prolonged period of time, putting families and communities at risk of a preventable illness, hospitalization, and death.”.

PAHO’s review examined measles spread starting January 20, 2025, when the first person became ill in a large West Texas outbreak, according to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC).

Sources indicate that CDC data show 5,412 confirmed measles cases this year as of November 12. That’s the highest annual total since 1991 and more than double the 2025 count of 2,289 cases.

Andi Shane, MD, chief of pediatric infectious diseases at Children’s Healthcare of Atlanta, called the U.S. losing measles elimination status “a public health alarm that we are not being effective and we’re not controlling measles as well.”.

Recent findings suggest that the measles virus is highly contagious. It spreads through the air when an infected person coughs or sneezes. People can catch it in a room up to two hours after an infected person has left, according to the CDC.

“There’s really been very little measles in the United States over the past 25 years until January 2025,” William Moss, MD, a professor of epidemiology at the Johns Hopkins Bloomberg School of Public Health, told Healthline.

Recent findings suggest that losing the status itself doesn’t change much about daily life for most Americans, Moss remarked. The concern is the measles outbreaks, hospitalizations and deaths behind the loss, he said.

He called the loss “a big red flag” after “enormous efforts over the past 26 years” to keep the status.

Sources indicate that A country loses its elimination status when there is “uninterrupted circulation of the same virus genotype and lineage for 12 months or more,” according to PAHO. Shane explained it this way: “For the past 12 months in the United States, we’ve had ongoing circulation of the measles virus and person-to-person transmission is occurring.”.

In a recent development, canada lost its elimination status in November 2025, and the U.K. and five European countries lost theirs earlier in 2026.

The U.S. can regain the status. “Other countries have done that,” Moss remarked. Brazil, which lost its status in 2019, regained it in November 2024. Venezuela, which lost its status in 2018, regained it in 2023, according to PAHO.

It has been revealed that before the measles vaccine, measles infected an estimated 3 million to 4 million Americans each year, according to the CDC. Among reported cases, about 400 to 500 people died each year, 48,000 needed hospital care, and 1,000 developed encephalitis, or brain swelling.

Here’s a timeline of measles elimination in the U.S.:.

Sources indicate that moss mentioned elimination efforts “really intensified” after a large outbreak from 1989 to 1992. Part of that push was “really promoting school entry vaccination checks,” he said.

“That was one of the key policy changes that I think allowed for measles elimination in the United States.”.

Every state and Washington, D.C., require children to be vaccinated against measles to attend school, though exemptions vary by state, according to the nonprofit health policy organization KFF.

Fewer kindergartners are getting the MMR vaccine, according to the CDC.

Kindergarten MMR coverage fell from 95.2% in the 2019–2020 school year to 92.4% in 2025–2026. About 280,000 kindergartners started the 2025–2026 school year without records showing they had completed the MMR series, the CDC reported.

Shane said “95 out of 100 people need to be protected against measles” for a community to get herd protection.

“So since we’ve been below that for many, many months, that is also contributing to the loss of our elimination status,” she stated.

Recent findings suggest that “It takes two things to have a measles outbreak,” Moss stated. A community needs low vaccine coverage, and someone with measles has to enter it and “start the chain of transmission,” he said.

About 96% of this year’s cases were among people who were unvaccinated or had unknown vaccination status, up from 93% in 2025, according to the CDC.

Moss said many of those cases are adults.

“This is particularly true in Pennsylvania, where about two-thirds of the cases are in adults,” he said. Many never got vaccinated as kids and grew up while measles was rare, so they never built natural immunity, he said.

In a recent development, he noted that having so many unvaccinated adults puts pregnant people and adults with chronic conditions like lung disease at risk of serious illness. The U.S. has already seen “dozens of pregnant women actually getting infected during pregnancy,” he remarked.Infected parents can also spread measles to young children and grandparents, Shane said. Shane traced much of the hesitancy to the pandemic. “With COVID there’s been an overall distrust in vaccines and vaccination that initially started with COVID but has now spread to other vaccines,” she said.

According to recent reports, moss pointed to the federal government. “We know what it takes to achieve and sustain elimination. We have the expertise. We have the resources,” he said.

According to recent reports, he cited staff cuts at the CDC and noted messaging from Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. and President Donald Trump has undermined vaccine confidence. He called federal messaging on vaccines “really mixed and weak.”.

Moss also criticized the President’s August 10 executive order calling for the MMR vaccine to be split into separate shots for each disease.

“There’s no justification for that, and those vaccines don’t even exist in the United States,” he said.

In a recent development, measles may cause ear infections, diarrhea, pneumonia, encephalitis and, in some cases, death, according to the CDC. The disease may also weaken the immune system for weeks to a year after recovery, raising the risk of flu, COVID-19, or RSV, Shane said. “It’s not a benign childhood disease,” Moss said.

The best protection against measles is two doses of the MMR vaccine, which are about 97% effective, according to the CDC. Shane noted, “There are not very many other things we do in life that give you such great protection.” People who missed doses can still catch up, she added. “If you just don’t know or can’t tell, there’s no harm — as long as you’re eligible — in getting another MMR vaccine.”.

Shane added that “parents really want to do the right thing for their children.”.

Recent findings suggest that “We know that the MMR vaccine — that’s the vaccine that provides protection against measles — is a safe vaccine. It’s a very effective vaccine,” Shane said.

It has been revealed that babies under 12 months are too young for the vaccine. “So they depend on the protection of the people around them,” Shane noted.

The CDC recommends a first MMR dose at 12 to 15 months and a second at 4 to 6 years. Babies 6 to 11 months old who will travel internationally should get an early dose, and adults without proof of immunity should get at least one dose, according to the CDC.

To stop the outbreaks, Moss mentioned the U.S. will need to “increase vaccine coverage, particularly in those communities that have had long-standing low vaccine rates.”.

Sources indicate that so far, the response has been “more reactive than proactive,” Moss said. Public health teams scramble once an outbreak starts, he said, and he wants more outreach to at-risk communities before measles arrives.

“I am worried about the ability of the United States to regain measles elimination status in the current climate,” Moss mentioned.

Latest Update: Mysterious volcanic rock discovered in the Mariana Trench

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (818 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Popsci

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Space exploration tends to suck up most of the oxygen when it comes to venturing out into the unknown.
  • That absurd depth and bone-crushing pressure make Challenger Deep brutally difficult to study.
  • Recent findings suggest that using the remotely operated Jason/Medea submarine robot, the team documented evidence of pyroclastic rocks (the shattered debris of violent eruptions) on the trench wall some 20,000 feet below the surface.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Space exploration tends to suck up most of the oxygen when it comes to venturing out into the unknown. But there’s an arguably even more mysterious frontier hidden beneath us. Nowhere is that more real than at Challenger Deep. The deepest known point on Earth, Challenger Deep is located in the 1,580-mile-long Mariana Trench at the floor of the Pacific Ocean. Getting to the bottom of this ancient chasm means diving more than 6.8 miles (around 36,000 feet) underwater. For a sense of scale, Mount Everest could be dropped into this chasm, and its summit still wouldn’t reach the surface.

That absurd depth and bone-crushing pressure make Challenger Deep brutally difficult to study. As a result, assumptions about what lies down there rarely hold up for long. Scientists long believed the area’s frigid, pitch-dark depths couldn’t sustain life, until a pair of divers reported animals near the seafloor in 1960. Now, a team using a robotic submersible in the trench says they have found the deepest evidence of explosive volcanic eruptions ever documented in the ocean.

Recent findings suggest that using the remotely operated Jason/Medea submarine robot, the team documented evidence of pyroclastic rocks (the shattered debris of violent eruptions) on the trench wall some 20,000 feet below the surface. Finding those kinds of rocks there was unexpected and will change the way geologists view the area. Writing today in the journal Frontiers in Earth Science, the researchers say their discoveries may also “help explain why the Challenger Deep is so deep.”.

“Explosive volcanism near trenches is unusual, so we were very surprised,” Dr. Robert J. Stern, a geologist at the University of Texas at Dallas and study co-author, said in a statement. “These are the deepest pyroclastic rocks documented to date from anywhere in the ocean.”.

Reaching the depth needed to study the Mariana Trench takes some serious equipment and preparation. In 2012, Titanic director James Cameron famously made the dive with a specially designed submersible that reportedly cost around $10 million to build. In this case, the team of scientists turned to a veteran robotic system called Jason/Medea. Part of the National Deep Submergence Facility and funded by the National Science Foundation, Jason/Medea traces its earliest version back to 1988. From the outside, the ROV somewhat resembles a Zamboni machine used to surface ice skating rinks.

The robot can operate as deep as 21,385 feet below the surface, thanks to a roughly six-mile long fiber-optic cable connecting it to a vessel on the surface. Jason is equipped with a video and still-imaging systems. Its footage travels up through Medea, a companion robot that  hangs slightly higher in the water to buffer Jason from the motion of the vessel above. In addition to taking photos and videos, Jason has mechanical arms he can use to collect rock and sediment samples. The robotic duo has completed hundreds of dives around the world, analyzing hydrothermal vents in the Atlantic and Pacific Ocean, and even visiting a 1,600-year-old sunken Roman trading ship.

Industry observers note that in this case, the scientists deployed their robot companion in late 2024 along a 341 mile segment of the trench near Challenger Deep. Over seven dives, the robot team covered around 186 miles, taking photos and videos along the way. Analyzing the footage, the human team determined that the eastern part of the stretch is deeper than the western part and has steeper trench walls. They came across the old volcanic rocks on that steeper western side, seen below arranged in a thin flat layer. Exactly where these rocks erupted from remains unclear.

”We haven’t identified the eruption sites yet,” Stern added. “We know that these hot pyroclastic flows moved down slopes, but we don’t think they moved very far. They retained enough heat to re-weld themselves into pretty hard rocks, and that heat would’ve been lost if the pyroclastic flows traveled great distances.”.

In a recent development, the unexpected rocks were only one part of the expedition. The team also set out to study fragments of older, exposed crust and mantle. They also tasked the robot with studying the Shinaki Seep Field, one of deepest known hydrothermal vents sites on the planet. There was some cleanup duty as well:  the team recovered fluid-sampling devices left behind by a previous group of Japanese scientists in 2016. Explorers have rather glibly documented human trash all the way down at the bottom of Challenger Deep but these scientists, at least, won’t be adding to the litter.

  • Industry observers note that the reason for the recall is that the “fuel flange joint assembly may have been improperly manufactured.” As a consequence, Honda says this could allow the fuel line connection to loosen and separate, ultimately resulting in a fuel leak and engine stall.
  • It has been revealed that honda says that when part production shifted locations, 67 replacement parts were produced without brazing material.

According to recent reports, it’s not too often we get newly introduced recalls for older cars like the Honda S2000, but today is one of those days. According to the National Highway Traffic Safety Administration, Honda is recalling 16,387 S2000 roadsters from the 2004–20005 model years, the first two years of the AP2 refresh. A quick look at the sales figures for those years seems to suggest that means all (or close to all) S2000s from those years are part of the recall population.

Industry observers note that the reason for the recall is that the “fuel flange joint assembly may have been improperly manufactured.” As a consequence, Honda says this could allow the fuel line connection to loosen and separate, ultimately resulting in a fuel leak and engine stall. The problem with manufacturing relates to whether or not it was built with brazing material at the joint-to-flange connection. With the part being a push-to-fit part, Honda says this lack of material could cause the connection to become loose and separate.

It has been revealed that honda says that when part production shifted locations, 67 replacement parts were produced without brazing material. These parts were shipped and potentially installed in S2000s. Honda estimates the percentage of cars with the defect is 1 percent. There won’t be many warning signs before it’s too late to continue driving, but Honda says stalling, a misfire, fuel odor and an inability to start the engine are all symptoms.

Sources indicate that as of now, Honda indicates there are no injuries or deaths related to this issue. Those with cars in the recall range will have to bring their convertibles into the Honda dealer for the remedy. Once there, it will receive a latest and improved fuel flange joint assembly free of charge.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The Illinois Clean Ports Program is putting $104 million behind efforts to help clean up its working waterfronts, funds earmarked for heavy-duty electric equipment assets that includes forklifts, giant reach stackers, switcher locomotives, and the charging equipment needed to support them. There’s even a passenger ferry!

According to recent reports, procurement is now underway for zero-emission vehicles, equipment, and supporting infrastructure at four sites across the state. Administered by the Illinois Environmental Protection Agency (Illinois EPA), Illinois’ Clean Ports Program aims to modernize operations at ports and waterfront facilities in Chicago, the Quad Cities, and southern Illinois’ river port districts.

In a recent development, “Illinois’ waterways are a competitive advantage for the state,” stated Illinois Governor JB Pritzker, who was elected to a historic third term on 03NOV. “By modernizing port infrastructure, advancing zero-emission technology, and improving air quality, we are strengthening our economy while building a cleaner future for Illinois.”.

Illinois’ Clean Ports Program isn’t just replacing diesel-powered equipment with electric alternatives – instead, the plan also includes Level 2 and DC fast charging, shore power and charging for electrified ships, and comprehensive grid upgrades designed to modernize existing port operations and support the deployment of newly introduced electric equipment.

The program takes a holistic approach to port electrification at Chicago’s Illinois International Port District (IIPD), treating energy generation, storage, and deployment as parts of a single connected system. On-site solar helps meet the port’s growing electricity needs while excess power is stored for peak hours, when grid electricity is most expensive. This setup reduces strain on the local grid, and acts as a hedge against rising energy costs.

For smaller public port districts, replacing aging equipment and upgrading electrical infrastructure can be an enormous financial undertaking. The Illinois Clean Ports Program helps make those investments possible, bringing cleaner, healthier, zero-emission technology within reach of terminal operators while preparing the state’s ports for a more competitive freight future.

This EV-Swapped 1967 Porsche 912 Has 300 HP And A Split Battery Pack

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Inverted is a name that's been around for a while in the EV-swap world.
  • According to Piston Heads, the owner of this specific 912 had already swapped a more potent 911 engine into its rear end, but wanted something even better suited for daily driving.
  • It has been revealed that there's some clever engineering here, too.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Inverted is a name that's been around for a while in the EV-swap world. It started out doing electric powertrain swaps for classic Range Rovers, which it still does. But it also has a bespoke program now, under which it will develop custom EV swaps for customers for any sort of car they want. In this specific case, Inverted stuffed some batteries and an electric motor into an old Porsche 912. Interestingly, this is the third powertrain that's been in this Porsche.

According to Piston Heads, the owner of this specific 912 had already swapped a more potent 911 engine into its rear end, but wanted something even better suited for daily driving. So they took their car to Inverted and the team got to work. The end result is a car that looks exactly like a normal Porsche 912, with all of its gorgeous old-school styling, but drives like a modern EV.

It has been revealed that there's some clever engineering here, too. The 62 kWh battery pack is more than enough to propel the vintage Porsche's featherweight body a fair ways. However, that's a lot of weight to hang over the rear axle. Air-cooled Porsches were already prone to lift-off oversteer, so they don't need any more. So Inverted came up with an interesting solution: split the pack into two parts. On section is mounted out back where the engine used to be, and the other is under the hood. It means the electric 912's weight balance is actually better than the original car's.

Inverted claims that this EV 912 has around 250 miles of range, and it can DC fast charge at 75 kW. The latter might seem weak in the world of modern EVs, but it's perfectly fine in a classic like this. This is a daily driver, not a long-distance cruiser. So 250 miles is more than enough for daily usage, and plugging it in overnight to charge will get the owner a fresh battery in the morning.

In a recent development, the rear-mounted electric motor makes 300 horsepower, so it's much more potent than the original 912 four-cylinder engine which made around 90 horsepower. Latest Update: New Guidelines Recommend Routine Prostate Cancer Screening for Men Over 50

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (993 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Healthline

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • As rates of advanced prostate cancer continue to rise, the American Cancer Society (ACS) has issued new guidelines recommending routine prostate cancer screening for many men starting at age 50.
  • The updated recommendations, published November 12 in CA: A Cancer Journal for Clinicians, mark a shift from the organization’s previous emphasis on shared decision making about whether to undergo screening.
  • Under the latest guidelines, the ACS recommends regular prostate-specific antigen (PSA) testing beginning at age 50 for men at average risk of prostate cancer and age 45 for those at higher risk.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

As rates of advanced prostate cancer continue to rise, the American Cancer Society (ACS) has issued new guidelines recommending routine prostate cancer screening for many men starting at age 50.

The updated recommendations, published November 12 in CA: A Cancer Journal for Clinicians, mark a shift from the organization’s previous emphasis on shared decision making about whether to undergo screening.

Under the latest guidelines, the ACS recommends regular prostate-specific antigen (PSA) testing beginning at age 50 for men at average risk of prostate cancer and age 45 for those at higher risk.

Advances in MRI technology and biomarker testing may also help doctors determine which men need further testing, potentially reducing unnecessary biopsies and overtreatment.

The ACS last updated its prostate cancer screening guidelines in 2010, when conflicting research findings raised questions about whether the benefits of PSA screening outweighed the potential harms.

At the time, the organization emphasized informed, shared decision making between patients and healthcare professionals.

However, longer-term follow-up studies have since provided stronger evidence of the benefits of early detection, prompting the ACS to conduct a systematic review and patch its recommendations.

The authors of the report noted, “In making these recommendations, we recognize that PSA testing is only the first step in a screening cascade that includes secondary testing of men with an elevated PSA level and treatment decisions for men diagnosed with prostate cancer.”.

The new guidelines recommend a PSA test every 2 years for men ages 50–69 with an average risk of prostate cancer.

The recommendation for those at high risk is a PSA test every year starting at age 45.

For men ages 70–74, the ACS recommends individualized decision making. If an individual chooses to be screened, the ACS recommends a PSA test every 2 years until the age of 74.

Ramkishen Narayanan, MD, Director of the Center for Urologic Health at The Roy and Patricia Disney Family Cancer Center at Providence Saint Joseph Medical Center in Burbank, CA, who wasn’t involved in the report, told Healthline that screening shouldn’t automatically be ruled out for men over 75.

“[A] point worth noting is that for men over 75, their PSA history as well as their individual clinical scenarios should be evaluated, and that PSA should not be discouraged in this group of men if their life expectancy and clinical history warrant a PSA check.”.

According to the ACS, approximately 1 in 8 men will be diagnosed with prostate cancer during their lifetime.

Individual risk depends on age, race/ethnicity, and other factors:.

Prostate cancer diagnoses in the United States increased by around 3% per year between 2014 and 2022, according to the ACS.

The rise in diagnoses, particularly advanced-stage prostate cancer, has renewed attention on the importance of regular screening.

In a recent development, “[The] current state of prostate cancer screening guidelines is vague and generalized. This has led to ambiguity, disagreement, and variation of opinion among healthcare providers and institutions in their approach to men’s health,” stated S. Adam Ramin, MD, board certified urologist, urologic oncologist, and medical director of Urology Cancer Specialists in Los Angeles, CA, who wasn’t involved in the report.

The updated ACS guidelines drew partly on findings from a 2025 follow-up of the European Randomized Study of Screening for Prostate Cancer (ERSPC), which found that regular PSA screening was associated with a 13% reduction in prostate cancer deaths over 23 years.

A 12-year ERSPC follow-up in 2012 also suggested that regular screening was associated with a decrease in metastatic prostate cancer diagnosis, which is another finding that influenced the updated guidance.

“Prostate cancer can take many years, even decades, to become clinically significant, so it takes a long time for us to see the consequences of changes in screening practices,” Taylor Goodstein, MD, assistant professor of urology in the College of Medicine at the University of Cincinnati, who wasn’t involved in the report, told Healthline.

“With longer follow-up from randomized trials, we now have more convincing evidence that PSA screening reduces the risk of dying from prostate cancer,” she noted.

“The ACS guidelines are important now because they drive home the most important point that prostate cancer screening saves lives,” noted Narayanan.

Healthcare professionals use PSA levels to help determine whether additional testing for prostate cancer may be necessary.

The ACS recommends further testing for men under 70 with PSA levels of 3 ng/mL or higher.

For those ages 70 and older, the ACS recommends further testing if their PSA is 6.5 ng/mL or higher. This is because PSA levels tend to be naturally higher in older men.

You can speak with your healthcare professional to find out more about PSA cutoff levels.

Goodstein told Healthline that the ways this new guidance can change the outlook for prostate cancer are simple.

“If we screen men, we can catch troublesome cancers early, before they have a chance to spread,” she mentioned.

Sources indicate that goodstein also emphasized how much the evaluation process has changed. In the past, an elevated PSA level often led directly to a biopsy.

Today, doctors generally repeat the PSA test within two weeks to three months to confirm the result. If PSA levels remain elevated, additional testing, including a prostate MRI or validated biomarker test, can help determine whether a biopsy is necessary.

Narayanan told Healthline, “The new guidelines will hopefully remove any confusion about the value of PSA screening and encourage prostate cancer screening as an integral part of a man’s ‘checkup’.”.

He added that it is worth noting that the DRE (digital rectal exam) adds little value to the initial prostate cancer screening and is no longer something that men should fear.

Sources indicate that “Adoption of this set of specific guidelines standardizes the approach to screening for prostate cancer. It provides a unified effort among all levels of healthcare. It most likely will increase the chances of finding prostate cancer in earlier stages and lead to improved cancer treatment outcomes,” mentioned Ramin.

In a recent development, one of the upcoming events is Flickering Flames, which comes with its own progression track of 25 levels. Content is, of course, unlocked using Merits, which are earned from XP in matches. The other event is the Candleberry Banquet Project, which requires you to donate items found on the surface (including Candleberries).

You’ll earn rewards each time, and each stage completed will reveal a upcoming scene on the banquet table. Likewise, there are cosmetic rewards as part of each stage, and you can use it as a source of Merits, too.

While on the subject, the upcoming revision also kicks off a new Raider Deck (battle pass). Available from December 26, The Goalie Raider Deck is pretty much what you’d expect. You’ll find several pages of cosmetic and useful items. The new Deck will be available to all players for free.

Fancy axes and simple pottery show how interconnected Europe was 5,000 years ago

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (526 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Popsci

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Today, the Rhine River stands as a physical border between parts of France and Germany, and a cultural boundary between Western and Central Europe.
  • In a recent development, sebastian Schultrich, an archaeologist at Kiel University in Germany, looked at late Neolithic coarse pottery, double axes, and collective graves from either side of the Rhine and found significant cross-boundary ties in the late 4th and early 3rd millennia BCE.
  • “The combination of pottery, burial rituals and tools reveals new insights into life 5,000 years ago,” Schultrich stated in a statement.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Today, the Rhine River stands as a physical border between parts of France and Germany, and a cultural boundary between Western and Central Europe. This physical and cultural separation seems to have existed for a very long time. Archaeological evidence on either side of the river as early as the late fourth millennia BCE reveals differences. Archaeologists have determined that the river is a sort of barrier during this time—but new research challenges this conclusion.

In a recent development, sebastian Schultrich, an archaeologist at Kiel University in Germany, looked at late Neolithic coarse pottery, double axes, and collective graves from either side of the Rhine and found significant cross-boundary ties in the late 4th and early 3rd millennia BCE. His findings, described in a study recently published in the archaeological journal Germania, suggest that populations in Western, Central, and Northern Europe were more connected than previously assumed.

“The combination of pottery, burial rituals and tools reveals new insights into life 5,000 years ago,” Schultrich stated in a statement.

The pottery in question, called coarse ware, is simple and plain—so much so that archaeologists have seen it as culturally insignificant. The roughly-shaped artifacts have emerged in many regions of Europe. It became widespread in modern-day central and northern France as well as the western Alpine region starting in the mid-4th millennium BCE. Afterward, it also became prominent in modern-day western and northern Germany and Denmark.

In a recent development, “There are indications that a convergence of pottery styles across such great distances occurred gradually and unconsciously. This is an indicator of high mobility within a region where there were no distinct barriers between groups, or where the boundaries were fluid,” said Schultrich.

Double stone axes—prestigious axes with two cutting edges and a shaft hole—were also widespread in this period. Archaeologists have discovered them from France through Central Europe to Scandinavia and Poland. While the dates of the French double stone axes has been a subject of contention, it’s currently clear that they, along with the Central and Northern European versions, hail from the the 4th and early 3rd millennia BCE. Unlike coarse ware, the double axe design seems to have been intentionally widespread, showing that a shared concept existed on either side of the river.

The same regions are also home to different versions of large-scale group burials, including passage graves or gallery graves. But they all were the final resting place of dozens to hundreds of individuals, were used over many generations, and were the locations of ritual acts and gatherings. This is more evidence of a shared idea, even though its regional manifestation differed.

“It was not a uniform cultural complex,” Schultrich explained. “What we see here is a network characterised by fundamental narratives, yet one that simultaneously allowed scope for strong regional peculiarities. This is an early example of a complex, differentiated form of society in which identity combined both supra-regional and local elements.”.

By drawing prehistoric connections across the Rhine, Schultrich revealed ties across late Neolithic Europe that clearly overcame the watery boundary.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, for decades, Briggs & Stratton has helped keep the lights on after the storm with its gas-powered generators. Now, the manufacturer is bringing that legacy to the electric age with a fresh 16 kWh backup battery designed to scale with your growing energy needs.

Briggs & Stratton partnered with Texas-based EG4 to offer an all American-branded solution for battery backup power solution last year, and its stackable SimpliPHI batteries helped make it easy to right-size home battery projects – but those batteries were limited in size, and limited in what they could actually offer. With the launch of the brand’s new, 16 kWh SimpliPHI battery, the organization is ready to meet your energy needs … even if those needs take you up to 512 kWh. (!).

For context, the average US home uses about 865 kWh of energy per month, so a 512 kWh battery should theoretically keep your lights on for nearly 18 days after a storm – or provide basic power for your whole block for a weekend, at least!

Sources indicate that “This launch represents a significant shift in our battery strategy,” explains Sequoya Cross, vice president of energy storage at Briggs & Stratton. “Our combined resources allow us to bring a competitively priced battery of the highest quality to energy storage installers.”.

An onboard battery management system (BMS) and built-in Wi-Fi gateway help to streamline the system’s setup for installers, while the Briggs battery’s automatic inverter sensing technology supports closed-loop communication with Sol-Ark, Solis, EG4, Growatt, Megarevo, Victron, and other leading inverters. Other installer-friendly features include an IP65-rated enclosure allows for indoor or outdoor installation in either ground- or wall-mounted setups without requiring an additional cabinet, and an integrated circuit breaker that allows technicians to isolate the battery during servicing.

According to recent reports, the battery itself is rated for 8,000 cycles at 90% depth of discharge, with a charge and discharge rate of 0.5C and an end-of-life capacity of 70%. Briggs & Stratton backs its latest battery packs with a 12-year parts warranty that includes labor and travel costs, as well as a US-based tech support service.

The SimpliPHI 16 is available for pre-order now, though pricing was not mentioned in the original press release.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that when people spend nearly $2 million on a two-seat, mid-engine car, you can safely assume it is not the only car in their garage.
  • But Spyker CEO Victor Muller has a different idea.
  • That's a refreshing philosophy from someone selling a car this pricey.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that when people spend nearly $2 million on a two-seat, mid-engine car, you can safely assume it is not the only car in their garage. It makes sense that it will not be driven every day; however, often times cars like this are not really driven at all. They spend their entire lives in climate-controlled garages, tucked beneath soft covers. And when the car in question is something like a one-of-25 C8 Preliator XXV Coupé, the temptation to preserve it as a collectible is understandable.

But Spyker CEO Victor Muller has a different idea. He wants his customers to get behind the wheel and drive. "We prefer to sell our cars to people that actually use them," Muller told me during an interview at Retromobile Fresh York. "Because that's what I made them for. To drive the hell out of them.".

That's a refreshing philosophy from someone selling a car this pricey. Particularly when that car is the newly introduced C8 Preliator XXV Coupé, which looks as much like a piece of fine jewelry as an 800-horsepower road rocket. Unfortunately, Muller admits that many of Spyker's previous creations haven't enjoyed particularly active lives.

It has been revealed that "Many of our cars, of the 252 we made so far, have just ended up in dungeons, in vaults, in spaces where nobody will ever see them," Muller said. He's hoping to change that by organizing more owner events and encouraging customers to spend time enjoying their cars; Spyker has joined the Supercar Owners Circle, a global network of car collectors, and is planning gatherings in Europe and the United States.

Recent findings suggest that the company is also in a position where it can be selective about who gets its cars. According to Muller, all 25 Preliator XXV Coupés sold during their debut at The Quail, a Motorsports Gathering in August. Every single one was snapped up in a day. "I've never seen anything like that in my entire life," he said. Spyker prepares to build 25 Spyders and 25 Sedancas in 2028, he added, once production of the Coupés is complete next year.

Who is buying these cars has changed dramatically over the last quarter century. "In 2000, my typical customer was a fifty-five to sixty-year-old industrialist—old money, car collector, very astute buyer," Muller explained. "Fast forward twenty five years. Your average age is thirty-five years. Tech investor. Huge collection. Knows his cars completely. But nobody asks how much it is.".

Recent findings suggest that muller says approximately 40 percent of his new buyers are existing or former Spyker owners, and roughly 80 percent of the new cars are expected to go to the United States. But no matter how old the buyer is or where they live, Muller wants them to drive the cars. This makes sense when you understand his approach to engineering; The new car has no massive infotainment screens or hybrid systems, and electronic intervention is largely limited to essential safety features like ABS and stability control.

Recent findings suggest that “If you mis-shift in a Spyker and you drive two hundred miles an hour and you shift to second gear, you blow up the engine," Muller mentioned. "And I think it has to be that way in Spyker world." For Spyker, the connection between driver and machine is more crucial than chasing lap records, acceleration figures and electronic nannies. "If you don't like that, buy something else," he added. "If not, man up—drive a Spyker.".

Industry observers note that another way to demonstrate that these cars are meant to be driven is to get the brand back into racing. Muller revealed that Spyker is taking steps toward returning to professional endurance competition. The firm competed in the 24 Hours of Le Mans eight times, most recently in 2010. Naturally, I asked whether another trip to Le Mans might be in Spyker's future.

Recent findings suggest that "Absolutely," Muller stated. "We'd love to go back in racing." Latest Update: Waymo Is Recalling Its Robotaxis Because They're Not Great At Dealing With Human Instructions

📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (961 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Insideevs

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, waymo recalled its robotaxis again on Friday, citing issues with navigating closed freeway lanes and handling manually controlled intersections.
  • Sources indicate that the company's robotaxis were banned from California freeways earlier this month after a few high-profile incidents.
  • It has been revealed that the robotaxis seem to be very adept at dealing with normal road conditions.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, waymo recalled its robotaxis again on Friday, citing issues with navigating closed freeway lanes and handling manually controlled intersections. For anyone who has been following Waymo closely, this shouldn't be that surprising.

Sources indicate that the company's robotaxis were banned from California freeways earlier this month after a few high-profile incidents. Waymo took the voluntary step of suspending interstate operation nationwide on Wednesday, meaning the entire fleet is now back to running primarily on local roads and minor state highways.

It has been revealed that the robotaxis seem to be very adept at dealing with normal road conditions. But the trouble seems to be when something unexpected pops up. Regulators from California cited poor behavior surrounding closed lanes and construction zones, a recurring problem for the organization, along with a another recent high-profile incident involving a California Highway Patrol rolling road block.

If you don't know what that last sentence means, you aren't alone. When I first moved to California a few years ago, I had no idea what a rolling road block or "traffic break" meant in normal parlance. But drive California freeways long enough and you'll experience one. A CHP cruiser or a group of them joins the highway, puts on its lights, and slowly zigzags across all lanes of traffic, blocking drivers from passing or exceeding the speed of the maneuver. The goal is typically to create a safe break in traffic for authorities to removed debris, clear and accident, or otherwise operate on the road. Sometimes it just slows down the herd before it barrels into a blind-corner accident scene at 80 mph.

When I first experienced this, I was plenty confused. But when I saw cops swerving in front of me with lights on, I naturally just slowed down and stayed behind me. Common sense told me that a cop swerving around with their lights on probably isn't looking for a race. Unfortunately, though, autonomous driving software doesn't always know how to interpret novel situations. So when a Waymo got caught behind a rolling road block, here's what it did:.

It has been revealed that yep, it tried to blow right by. CHP was able to hold it back, but I've seen a Trooper controlling six lanes of traffic with one car before. Add in an inventive and disobedient robotaxi and you can see how it could create a dangerous situation wherein an autonomous vehicle is driving down a road that construction workers or police think is effectively closed.

Now, Waymos are good enough at avoiding hitting things that I don't expect this would have been too bad. But even a small chance of a runaway robotaxi is unacceptable to regulators and to Waymo, so it's good to pause freeway operations until they figure things out.

Sources indicate that but the road block situation is indicative of a larger matter with autonomous vehicles, and perhaps the most interesting one. We think of driving as a predominantly legal or process-driven endeavor. You stop at stop signs, obey the speed limit, and keep it between the lines. Errors happen, but we tend to see them as based on improperly applied rules.

Yet the police here are disrupting the rules and enforcing an unscheduled and ad-hoc temporary speed limit and traffic flow. If you're from out of state or haven't experienced it yet, it's confusing, as there's direct ruleset for an impromptu situation like that. Yet any other driver caught in this situation wouldn't blow past the cop car. Like me, they'd approach it cautiously, and let the police car take the lead.

According to recent reports, that is the matter I'm referring to: Driving is not just about rules and infrastructure. It's a social behavior. We wave each other ahead at stop signs and intersections. We signal our intent for an aggressive merge by riding the side of the lane market. You look at people's faces to gaze intention and attention. And when the traffic lights are down or the road is blocked by falling trees, we create impromptu order where chaos exists, nodding or waving to signal that it's someone else's term.

Recent findings suggest that this was always going to be the hard part for robotaxis. That's why the same recall applies to another troubled behavioral pattern for Waymos: They struggle when officers or city workers are manually controlling and intersection. Whether it's due to a high-traffic event or an outage, it's not all that uncommon to see a police officer directing traffic by hand. They wave you through or hold you back.

It has been revealed that but what happens if the car loses sight of the person directing traffic? What if the person directing traffic isn't actually a police officer, and waves you through a red light? What if the alternate route the police point you to spits the robotaxi onto a highway, where it isn't allowed to go?

It has been revealed that there are a million more what-ifs related to this social component of driving. All of them will have to be encountered and solved as they come, just as you and I eventually figured these things out. Recall by recall, we'll turn these Waymos into upstanding citizens.

Mind Games: My ‘Secret’ to Enjoying Coffee Without Anxiety

💡 Key Takeaways
  • This article is part of a mental health content series called “Mind Games,” in which Healthline editor Morgan Mandriota draws on personal experience and research to challenge misconceptions, reduce stigma, review trends, and share hot takes and lessons learned about what it means to be mentally well.
  • Coffee and I don’t exactly have the best relationship.
  • Recent findings suggest that my morning cup tends to give me jitters, worsen my anxiety, and keep me up until 2 a.m.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

This article is part of a mental health content series called “Mind Games,” in which Healthline editor Morgan Mandriota draws on personal experience and research to challenge misconceptions, reduce stigma, review trends, and share hot takes and lessons learned about what it means to be mentally well.

Coffee and I don’t exactly have the best relationship.

Recent findings suggest that my morning cup tends to give me jitters, worsen my anxiety, and keep me up until 2 a.m. if I drink it past noon. As an already anxious human, the last thing I need is to exacerbate my symptoms, even if it’s coming from a delicious source.

Over a year ago, I noticed that my anxiety was higher than usual. I was also tossing and turning and waking up at all hours of the night for weeks on end.

Industry observers note that one night in particular, I woke up every hour for 8 hours. Naturally, I wanted to blame it on the full moon or anything other than my beloved coffee, but alas, I realized that my caffeine consumption was the most likely culprit.

Could I have aimed to set a strict drinking schedule to see if that fixed things? Sure. But instead, I decided to quit cold turkey and undergo an experiment to see how I’d feel going coffee-free for the first time in years.

According to recent reports, over the next 8 months, I’d swap my coffee station for a matcha setup, dabble in exotic herbal blends from my local teahouse, and become a self-proclaimed tea connoisseur. Lo and behold, my anxiety eased up, and my sleep quality improved, too.

Industry observers note that fast forward to 4 months ago, when I hopped back on the coffee train. But this time, I’m relying on a handy amino acid to help avoid anxiety and other unwanted side effects: L-theanine.

Health and wellness touch everyone’s life differently. This is one person’s story. The views and opinions expressed are those of the speaker and do not necessarily reflect the views or positions of Healthline Media and should not serve as a substitute for medical advice from a healthcare professional.

Recent findings suggest that L-theanine is mainly found in green and black tea and one type of wild mushroom. The mental health benefits of L-theanine consumption are an emerging area of research, but one 2024 review found that consuming around 200 to 400 milligrams (mg) may help relieve symptoms in people with anxiety disorders.

Still, anecdotal reports suggest there may be benefits of adding L-theanine to coffee. Over the last 5 years, the combo has been gaining traction on Reddit and TikTok for managing caffeine-related side effects.

Despite an overwhelming amount of rave reviews online, I couldn’t find much research to support these claims, so I spoke with a neurologist to see if they had any thoughts.

“This trend has real science behind it,” said Fawad Mian, MD, who is board certified in neurology, clinical neurophysiology, and sleep medicine and the founder of Ascend Regenerative.

“Controlled studies show caffeine plus L-theanine improves focus and attention more than caffeine alone, and some suggest it softens caffeine’s side effects, like tiredness, headaches, and blood pressure spikes,” Mian said. “It smooths caffeine’s effects but doesn’t erase them, so it’s not a license to drink more coffee,” he added.

With all of this in mind, especially after realizing just how calm I was while drinking black and green teas during my coffee break, I decided to give it a try.

After about 4 months of “testing,” I’ve found that adding L-theanine to my coffee works extremely well for me.

Industry observers note that no more anxiety, scatterbrain, shakiness, or staying up until 3 a.m. And no lifestyle overhaul needed. The supplement, which I prefer in liquid form, has become a seamless addition to my daily routine.

Every morning, I make a fresh batch of French press coffee with (strong) local beans, then I squeeze some L-theanine into my cup.

I’ve noticed that I get the usual coffee benefits like improved focus and concentration, plus a nice, calm, stable energy throughout the day.

Even if I drink it until 2 p.m., I’m fighting to keep my eyes open at night before I finally fall asleep around 10. Perhaps this is because L-theanine may also support quality sleep.

Mindful L-Theanine Drops is the liquid supplement that I use every day.

According to recent reports, I add a one-second squeeze (which contains 200 mg of L-theanine) into my morning coffee, then I’m good to go. I even started carrying a bottle in my bag just in case I get a latte from a coffee shop on a whim.

Industry observers note that you can also add it to a glass of water, a cup of tea, or another drink of your choosing. It’s unflavored, so it doesn’t alter the taste of your drinks. Real secret stuff.

Out of curiosity, and because I’m a natural skeptic and overthinker, I asked Mian if my positive experience could be a placebo effect, or if I’m seeing real results.

According to recent reports, “Expectation may play a small role, but the effect is biologically plausible,” he remarked. “L-theanine boosts calming brain activity that offsets caffeine’s stimulation, and 200 mg matches the doses used in studies.” However, he noted that it doesn’t speed caffeine clearance, so drinking coffee only in the morning still matters for sleep quality.

While L-theanine is generally safe to consume, it’s best to speak with a healthcare professional first, especially if you’re pregnant, nursing, receiving cancer treatment, or taking blood pressure medication or sedatives.

“Choose a third-party tested brand, and if caffeine makes you anxious, cutting back is still the simplest fix,” Mian added.

According to recent reports, so, if you’re anything like me and drinking coffee also leads to anxiety and jitters for you, I highly recommend trying this supplement once you get the green light from your doctor. It’s been working for me. It may work well for you, too.

Breaking: Albatross couple George and Geraldine lay an egg

⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that A bird couple with a long history has laid their first (and likely only) egg of the 2026-2027 season.
  • According to Friends of Midway Atoll, the pair did not produce an egg last year, making this arrival “especially exciting news.”.
  • Short-tailed albatrosses are almost completely white and have a large pink bill.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that A bird couple with a long history has laid their first (and likely only) egg of the 2026-2027 season. United States Fish and Wildlife Service (FWS) volunteer and photographer Dan Rapp spotted the egg on George and Geraldine’s nest this weekend. The pair are endangered short-tailed albatrosses (Phoebastria albatrus) or makalena in Hawaiian, and this is their 10th straight year together.

According to Friends of Midway Atoll, the pair did not produce an egg last year, making this arrival “especially exciting news.”.

Short-tailed albatrosses are almost completely white and have a large pink bill. The monogamous birds can live up to 50 years, and nest on islands and atolls where they typically lay one egg per season. Short-tailed albatrosses are listed as endangered, and biologists estimate that there are only 10,000 left in the wild.

It has been revealed that george and Geraldine were banded as chicks on Torishima Island, Japan. They raised their first chick together during the 2018–2019 breeding season. The duo is the only breeding pair of short-tailed albatross on the Midway Atoll, but other members of their species were observed last season. After spending the summer/non-nesting season apart, George was first spotted at Midway Atoll on October 18. He was reunited with Geraldine by October 22.

This remote group of islands sit about 1,250 miles from Hawaii’s capital Honolulu and are most famous for a pivotal World War II battle. Every fall, it becomes a temporary home to the world’s largest albatross colony. Albatrosses are a group of large migratory seabird species. Some notable albatross species are the wandering albatross (Diomedea exulans), which has the largest wingspan of any living bird species and the Laysan albatross (Phoebastria immutabilis). At over 70 years old, a Laysan albatross named Wisdom claims the title of oldest known banded wild bird. She has produced roughly 50 to 60 eggs, and as many as 30 of her chicks have fledged in her lifetime, and she became a grandmother once again in March. Wisdom has not been spotted yet this nesting season.

Bird enthusiasts from around the world can eavesdrop on this albatross colony via live cameras and follow Friends of Midway Atoll National Wildlife Refuge for updates. Viewers can expect to see the birds return to the islands, perform courtship dances, begin to nest, lay their eggs, and eventually watch fluffy albatross chicks.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • An 83 year old Congressional representative who sent an embarrassing letter to a well-meaning 10 year old constituent on the topic of electric cars and climate change, where she seems to brag about saddling his generation with debt through a recent climate rollback she voted for, has lost her seat.
  • Industry observers note that update: This article was originally posted on May 14, but we wanted to update it with news of the election result.
  • Christian Mango is ten years old, and was encouraged by his elementary school class to write a letter about a topic of his choice, and mail it to a decisionmaker.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

An 83 year old Congressional representative who sent an embarrassing letter to a well-meaning 10 year old constituent on the topic of electric cars and climate change, where she seems to brag about saddling his generation with debt through a recent climate rollback she voted for, has lost her seat.

Industry observers note that update: This article was originally posted on May 14, but we wanted to update it with news of the election result. After a recount, Chuck Hubbard has defeated Virginia Foxx by 330 votes, and will go on to represent NC-5 in Congress.

Christian Mango is ten years old, and was encouraged by his elementary school class to write a letter about a topic of his choice, and mail it to a decisionmaker. Christian chose his Congressional representative, 83 year old Virginia Foxx.

Foxx is an 11-term Congresswoman in North Carolina, one of the most gerrymandered states in the nation, and was expected to win a 12th term in the heavily republican district, having previously proudly touted an endorsement from an enemy of the US who tried to overthrow the government. Her opponent is Democrat Chuck Hubbard, a former journalist and native of the district.

For the topic of his letter, Christian chose electric cars – which is what makes this story relevant to us here at Electrek. Christian laid out several points about EVs, stating that “they’re better than normal cars. They’re better for the environment. They pay less. And there’s no gas.” (All true! well done Christian).

Christian suggested that electric cars could be incentivized with a $5,000 tax rebate – lower than the $7.5k EVs used to get, but better than the $0 they get federally today (compare to the ~$20k in ignored costs that gas cars still benefit from).

Christian went on to suggest action on climate change, stating “maybe there is still a chance for 6.5 million people to not die anymore and for the weather to get better just maybe glaciers stop melting.” Christian was probably referring to the number of people who die from air pollution globally each year (though several estimates suggest that number is actually higher, and Christian did conflate climate and weather… but we’ll give him a pass on this one, his heart is in the right place).

Recent findings suggest that christian was proud of his letter, as was his mother, Emily Mango, who noted “he researched, cited facts, and made good arguments in his essay – an essay that had nothing to do with politics. He was proud of his essay.”.

According to recent reports, but then he got a response, and that’s when things took a turn for the worse. Christian’s mother Emily angrily shared the response on Instagram, where it gained traction.

Emily remarked Foxx’s screed was “disrespectful, hostile and unkind” and called it “demoralizing and reprehensible.” She said she had to speak to her son and teach him that this response was “not okay,” and that “nobody should talk to a child like that and nobody should talk to a teacher like that.”.

I’d also add that it’s full of disinformation, and that it even seems to brag about the massive debt that Foxx has imposed on Christian’s generation.

In a recent development, foxx includes six links, all from propaganda publications that deny the science of climate change. 3 are from from WSJ (2 of which are opinion pieces) and 1 is from Fox, both of which are owned by the same climate denier, Rupert Murdoch. 1 is from Washington Times, a tabloid founded by a religious cult (yes, really), and 1 is from another right-wing climate denying publication, National Review.

Notably, none of the six links have anything to do with electric cars.

In the text of the response, Foxx touts republicans’ “all of the above” energy policy, which is ironic given that the party whose energy policy she touts has spent most of the last year forcing broken dirty coal plants open (which they are still doing after ruled illegal) and trying to shut down clean cheap ones. Apparently “all of the above” is code for “fossil fuels and nothing else.”.

Sources indicate that foxx’s letter does not directly address the strengths of electric cars, despite them being the subject of Christian’s letter. Notably, EVs actually can receive energy from any generation method, whether it be wind, solar, or even coal or gas – whereas gas-powered vehicles can only use one type of energy, oil. Thus, an “all of the above” strategy should probably find EVs the preferable route for transportation.

But in apparent contradiction to Foxx’s surely sincerely held belief that we should pursue an “all of the above” energy policy – which electric cars would help to achieve – she in fact has voted against EVs when given the opportunity.

Foxx claims in her response that she can’t support tax credits on electric cars, because those go to “mostly people with higher incomes who are able to purchase ‘fresh’ electric cars.”.

Recent findings suggest that but she in fact voted against, and later voted to repeal, incentives which were limited to lower-income-earners and were only available on cars up to a certain MSRP cap. Further, they were available on used vehicles, not just latest ones – suggesting that Foxx doesn’t know what she voted against.

Industry observers note that foxx was one of 218 republicans to vote in favor of a ~$4 trillion giveaway to wealthy elites. Her vote raised electric bills and threatened US energy security and surrendered US manufacturing jobs to China. Some of the money given away to wealthy elites in the bill was clawed back from energy efficiency programs that had been going to regular Americans.

Those energy efficiency programs had been instituted by the Inflation Reduction Act, the Biden-era law which established tax credits for EVs and other efficiency rebates. The Inflation Reduction Act was actually revenue positive, which is to say it reduced the national debt (by $238B), rather than adding to it, because of provisions to increase enforcement against wealthy tax cheats.

But most of the IRA was repealed by the bill that Foxx voted for, meaning the US lost out on those deficit reductions. All in all, the bill Foxx voted for would add $4 trillion to the national debt – which, incidentally, is another point Foxx touches on in her response.

In one sentence, she seems to directly mock Christian, telling him that “YOU and your classmates will be responsible for that debt” as part of a warning about the dangers of government debt.

But I read this sentence as mockery, rather than as a sincere warning, given that Foxx voted to add $4 trillion to the national debt, which she, at 83 years old, knows she will not have to pay off. Christian, who is 10, will likely spend his whole life saddled with the debt Foxx voted for.

He will also have to pay for her inaction on climate change, which will have increasingly worse effects on the world Christian will grow up into. Foxx’s generation has already felt the heat, with the massive floods that devastated her state in 2024, from a hurricane that was made 200x more likely due to climate change. Now, imagine how much worse it could get if Foxx’s policies remained in place until 72 years from now when Christian will be her age.

Foxx then closes out the letter with disparaging remarks about teachers, claiming that they are “too interested in indoctrinating you,” and warning Christian about “propaganda.” Which I guess indicates where Foxx’s attitude comes from – if she has spent her 83 years never trusting anyone who knows more than her about a topic, that would certainly lead to the ignorance reflected in her letter.

Foxx – who somehow has a doctorate in education and at the moment sits on the Congressional education committee – could have turned this into a nice moment to teach the child who wrote her something about democracy and responsive government, but instead turned it into a moment to teach the world what’s wrong with her.

When we first wrote this article in May, Foxx had a projected 97% chance of winning in a district which voted for her by a 19% margin in 2024.

But that was before America (and its short memory) was reminded of how incapable republicans are of leading anything.

After a pile of economic crises caused by Donald Trump’s incompetent “leadership,” and his continued participation in an 8-month-and-counting war of choice that is spiking energy prices worldwide, bringing oil profits to record highs (and attempting to distract the news from talking about the Epstein files, which he is heavily featured in and has tried to cover up), America was once again fed up. And his incompetence took his entire party down with him.

Safe republican seats were flipped around the country in the biggest “wave” election we’ve seen in recent times, with the Democrats gaining control of both the House and Senate.

And it looks like Democrat Chuck Hubbard, a Wilkes county native and former journalist, who also ran against Foxx in 2024, will now get his chance to represent the people of North Carolina’s 5th district, after winning by 330 votes in a recount.

The situation in North Carolina is particularly interesting, given that republicans had done an emergency redraw of district lines in an attempt to cheat their way to winning more seats.

Generally, district lines get redrawn after each Census, which happens on the decade mark, rather than mid-decade. But republicans saw ahead of time that they were likely to lose the House due to their unpopularity, and wanted to fudge the numbers in several states instead of going for a fair fight.

So they engaged in Gerrymandering, a process wherein district lines are redrawn to favor a particular political party. The idea is to put as many of your opponents’ votes into a few safe seats as possible, while spreading out your own votes to a wider range of seats that you win each by a small margin.

Foxx’s main argument against Christian’s suggested $5,000 EV incentive, is increasing national debt. Yet in just one tax bill, her approval increases the national debt over 10%. This is not Christian’s “responsibility”, this burden is forced on him, along with climate change.

But it turns out that republicans were even more unpopular than they thought, and as a result, their Gerrymandering backfired. Those narrow margins they sought ended up flipping more seats than would have otherwise flipped, turning North Carolina almost completely blue in what analysts have called a “Dummymander“. (NC-5 itself was not one of the redrawn districts, though – it just swung 19 whole points to the Dems).

After a nail-bitingly close election, Foxx requested a recount. The margin is extremely thin, just 0.12% of votes, but today Foxx called to concede, making it the last decided House race of the election, giving Democrats a 258-seat majority.

According to recent reports, foxx previously vowed to run again in 2028, hoping for a less hostile political environment. She will be 85 years old at the time of that election.
